young.html: A young man named Meno asks Socrates a question: Can goodness be taught? Socrates says he can't answer that, because he doesn't even know what goodness is. Can Meno tell him?

Meno tries, but every answer has a problem. He gets frustrated and says talking to Socrates is like touching an electric fish: it leaves you numb! Then he asks a tricky question: how can you search for something if you don't know what it is? Even if you found it, how would you know?

Socrates answers with an experiment. He calls over a boy who has never studied geometry. He draws a square in the sand and asks: how can we make a square exactly twice as big? The boy guesses wrong twice. But Socrates never tells him the answer. He only asks questions, and in the end the boy sees it for himself: build the new square on the line from corner to corner, the diagonal.

young.name: gb-meno-square
young.cap: Follow the boy's guesses and then the answer, one step at a time.

young.html: Double a square with paper. Cut out a paper square. Fold it corner to corner both ways, so the creases make an X. Now fold each corner in to the center. You have a new square with half the area. Unfold it: the original square is double the folded one, and the folded square's side runs along the diagonal of a quarter of the big one. Can you explain why to someone else, using only questions?

Socrates thought this showed that the boy already had the knowledge somewhere inside him, and the questions helped him remember it. Not everyone agrees with that idea. But everyone agrees the boy learned something real.

full.html: The Meno (about 385 BC) is short and lively. Meno is a wealthy young man from Thessaly, in northern Greece, visiting Athens; he has studied with the famous speaker Gorgias. He opens with no warm-up at all:

full.text: Meno. Can you tell me, Socrates, whether virtue is acquired by teaching or by practice; or if neither by teaching nor by practice, then whether it comes to man by nature, or in what other way?
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: “Virtue” here translates the Greek aretē: excellence, being good at being a person. Socrates says he can't say how virtue is acquired until he knows what it is.

items: A list: a man's virtue is managing the city's affairs, a woman's is managing a household, and so on. Socrates says he asked for one thing and got a swarm, like asking what a bee is and being shown many bees.
The power to rule. But is that a virtue in a child, or in someone who rules unjustly?
Wanting good things and being able to get them, justly. But justice is part of virtue, so the definition uses what it is trying to define.

full.text: …you seem to me both in your appearance and in your power over others to be very like the flat torpedo fish, who torpifies those who come near him and touch him, as you have now torpified me, I think. For my soul and my tongue are really torpid, and I do not know how to answer you…
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: The torpedo fish is the electric ray. Socrates replies that he numbs others only because he is numb himself: he is puzzled too.

Meno's paradox: you cannot search for what you know (you already have it) or for what you do not know (you would not know what to look for, or recognize it if you found it). So inquiry seems impossible.

Socrates answers with a teaching he says he heard from priests and poets: the soul is immortal and has learned everything before; so what we call learning is really recollection. He offers to show it.

Socrates calls over one of Meno's servants, a boy who speaks Greek but has never studied geometry (he was a slave, as many household servants in Athens were). Socrates draws a square with sides of two feet and asks for the side of a square twice the size.

full.name: gb-meno-square
full.cap: The lesson as Plato tells it: two wrong guesses, then the diagonal.

full.title: Why the diagonal works
full.q: A square has side 2, so area 4. Show that the square built on its diagonal has area 8.
steps: Put four copies of the square together to make a big square of side 4 and area 16.
Draw the diagonal of each small square so the four diagonals form a tilted square inside.
Each diagonal cuts its small square in half, and the tilted square is made of four halves: $4 \times 2 = 8$.
So the square on the diagonal is twice the original. (In modern terms, the diagonal is $2\sqrt2 \approx 2.83$, and $(2\sqrt2)^2 = 8$.)

full.html: When the boy's guesses fail, Socrates points out that he is now better off: before he thought he knew, now he knows that he doesn't, and he will want to find out. At the end, Socrates draws the lesson:

full.text: …for as all nature is akin, and the soul has learned all things, there is no difficulty in her eliciting or as men say learning, out of a single recollection all the rest, if a man is strenuous and does not faint; for all enquiry and all learning is but recollection.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: Thinking the boy just guessed until he got lucky. Every step is a question the boy answers by looking at the drawing. Whether that is “recollection” is a philosophical claim; that the boy reasoned his way there is plain in the text.

Socrates now reasons from a hypothesis, as geometers do: if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it can be taught. But then there should be teachers of it. Anytus, an Athenian politician who will later be one of Socrates' accusers, joins in and angrily rejects the paid teachers called sophists. Socrates points out that even famous good Athenians, like Pericles, did not manage to make their sons good.

So Socrates suggests that good leaders may act on true opinion rather than knowledge. True opinion guides you as well as knowledge does, as long as it lasts, but it is like the moving statues of the legendary sculptor Daedalus: it runs away unless it is tied down. Working out the reason why ties it down and turns it into knowledge.

Knowledge vs. true opinion: a person who has been to Larissa and someone who has only guessed the right road will both get you there. The difference is that knowledge is tied down by a reason and stays put. Philosophers still discuss this distinction.

deep.html: The Meno links the early dialogues, where Socrates questions and nobody reaches an answer, with Plato's bigger theories. Recollection returns in the Phaedo as an argument for the soul. The geometry example points to the Republic, where mathematics trains the mind to see beyond the senses. And the question “what is knowledge, and how does it differ from true opinion?” is the subject of the Theaetetus.

Aristotle mentions the Meno's puzzle in his Posterior Analytics and gives his own answer: we know some things in a general way and others in particular, so we can learn from what we partly know. Much later, the question of whether some knowledge is inborn divided the rationalists (Descartes, Leibniz) from the empiricists (Locke, Hume). Teachers today speak of “Socratic questioning” when they lead students to find answers themselves, as in this lesson.

items: Did the boy learn geometry, or remember it, or work it out? What would count as evidence?
Can goodness be taught? If so, by whom: parents, teachers, books, friends?
Why might knowing why something is true make it stick better than just knowing that it is true?

questions: Can goodness be taught? Think of someone who taught you to be kind or honest. How did they do it?
Is it better to be told an answer, or to work it out with help? When is each one better?
The boy felt stuck before he found the answer. Have you ever felt stuck right before you learned something?
What is the difference between guessing the right answer and knowing it?
Meno said Socrates was like an electric fish. Is it a good thing to be puzzled? Why?
